thread.title: World Bank report highlights Uganda's economic growth driven by agriculture but warns of fiscal risks
thread.title_full: World Bank report highlights Uganda's economic growth driven by agriculture but warns of fiscal risks

author: Globe Banner
title: World Bank report highlights Uganda's economic growth driven by agriculture but warns of fiscal risks
text:
Uganda’s economy grew by 6.3% in the fiscal year 2024/2025, up from 6.1% the previous year, according to the World Bank’s latest Uganda Economic Update. The report attributes this growth to a recovery in household consumption, increased government spending, and ongoing investment.
Growth was observed across agriculture, industry, and services sectors due to strong domestic demand and improved performance in agriculture and tourism. As a result, poverty is estimated to have declined during this period. However, fiscal pressures have risen with a widening deficit and higher debt-servicing costs. The report notes that “there is a need to focus on enhancing domestic revenue mobilization, and rebalancing spending toward education, health, and infrastructure while safeguarding debt sustainability and ensuring macroeconomic stability.”
The Uganda Economic Update is published twice yearly as an analysis of recent economic trends and future outlooks for the country. This edition projects continued positive growth over the medium term. Fiscal and external deficits are expected to improve gradually with moderating spending after elections, oil revenues starting in 2027, continued export strength, and sustained foreign direct investment inflows. Inflation is forecasted to remain low due to prudent monetary policy and stable commodity prices.
Poverty reduction is expected to continue into 2026 and 2027. Risks include possible fiscal slippages, delays in oil sector development, reduced overseas assistance, global uncertainty affecting commodity prices or financial conditions, climate shocks such as droughts or floods impacting rain-fed agriculture.
The report emphasizes agro-industrialization as key for economic transformation but notes that Uganda lags behind regional peers because of structural challenges:
1. Weak foundations in primary production due to low use of modern inputs like fertilizer or irrigation.
2. Weak governance leading to poor coordination and limited enforcement.
3. Limited access to finance for agriculture alongside high interest rates and poor infrastructure.
4. High vulnerability to climate shocks threatening productivity.
Three main recommendations are outlined:
1. “Strengthen foundations and infrastructure,” including climate-smart agricultural technologies; investing in irrigation; improving rural roads, energy supply; developing skills; enabling digital solutions for agricultural services.
2. “Improve the policy and enabling environment by reforming policies,” strengthening institutions; supporting farmer cooperatives; encouraging competition among private sector players; harmonizing regional trade policies.
3. “Mobilize private capital and market linkages by scaling up innovative financing,” leveraging digital platforms; enhancing trade competitiveness through value-chain financing instruments such as lease-to-own guarantees or blended finance.
The World Bank operates globally across more than 190 countries through five affiliated institutions providing loans and expertise for development initiatives (https://www.worldbank.org). Its work includes supporting sustainable economic growth—such as efforts highlighted in this update—and reducing poverty by improving social safety nets (https://www.worldbank.org). The organization collaborates with governments like Uganda’s along with other partners worldwide (https://www.worldbank.org).
Ajay Banga served as president of the World Bank (https://www.worldbank.org), which is owned by its member countries through their representatives on governing boards (https://www.worldbank.org). Since its founding at Bretton Woods in 1944 (https://www.worldbank.org), the institution has shifted focus from post-war reconstruction toward broader global development goals including poverty alleviation (https://www.worldbank.org).
